input.command:
cat > /home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles/patches/hyprland-activation-token-over-ipc.patch <<'HDR'
Add `hyprctl activationtoken`, so a keybind can hand an app permission to raise
itself.

Clicking a notification raises the app: the notification daemon mints an
xdg-activation token, sends it over D-Bus, and the app calls
xdg_activation_v1.activate(token, its_own_surface). The app picks the surface,
which is why the right window comes forward. Invoking the same action from a
keybind cannot do this -- the token must be requested by a Wayland client, and
`makoctl` is a D-Bus caller with no client, no seat and no input serial.

Hyprland 0.56.2 does not actually check the serial (CXDGActivationToken's
setSetSerial stores it and the commit handler never reads it), so today a daemon
can mint a token with any serial and this works by accident. 156276e51
("protocols/activation: reject invalid serials", #16427, 2026-09-30) closes
that, correctly -- it is a focus-stealing hole -- and ships with a hyprtester
suite, so unlike the 2025 attempt that was reverted a day later (d9cf1cb78 ->
0ed880f3f) it is likely to stick. When it releases, every keybind-driven
activation stops working, with no config to turn it off.

The usual fallback is to focus the window from outside with `dispatch
focuswindow` on a pid or class match. That is worse, not equivalent: one process
routinely owns several windows (a browser and its PWAs, an app with a main and a
preferences window), and the notification daemon has strictly less information
about which one is meant than the application does. Activation keeps the choice
with the app.

So let hyprctl mint one. The command exists on the IPC socket, which is already
how the user drives the compositor.

This grants no authority the caller did not have:

  - Anything that can reach the socket can already run
    `hyprctl dispatch focuswindow`, which focuses unconditionally.
  - CWindow::activate() is strictly weaker than that dispatcher: it honours
    misc:focus_on_activate, per-window suppressevent activate rules, and no-ops
    on unmapped windows, none of which focuswindow respects.
  - The token is single-use -- the activate request erases it from m_sentTokens
    -- and expires in 10 seconds rather than the 12 months a client token gets,
    since it is meant to be spent by the next command in a pipeline.
  - Tokens minted here share a null client, so they are capped at 10 the same
    way the commit handler caps a client's own.

Callers should keep the token out of argv, where any same-uid process can read
it from /proc/<pid>/cmdline, and pipe it instead.

input.command:
git add patches/hyprland-activation-token-over-ipc.patch patches/mako-activation-token-for-dbus-invoke.patch home.nix hyprland.nix && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
hyprctl activationtoken: survive Hyprland's incoming serial check

`makoctl invoke` raises the app today only by accident. Hyprland 0.56.2 never
reads the serial on an xdg-activation token request -- setSetSerial stores it
and the commit handler ignores it -- so mako's mint succeeds whatever it passes.

156276e51 ("protocols/activation: reject invalid serials", #16427) landed
2026-09-30 and closes that. It is right to: any client being able to mint a
token and raise itself unprompted is a focus-stealing hole. But 0.56.2 is still
the newest release and is two months old, the commit ships with a 689-line
hyprtester suite (unlike the 2025 attempt reverted a day later, d9cf1cb78 ->
0ed880f3f), and it adds no config to opt out. On the next bump, every
keybind-driven activation silently stops raising anything.

The cached pointer-enter serial already in the mako patch covers that only if
the pointer has crossed a notification since mako started, which for a
keyboard-driven workflow can be never. Falling back to `dispatch focuswindow`
on a pid or class match is strictly worse than activation, not equivalent: one
process routinely owns several windows and the daemon knows less about which is
meant than the app does.

So mint the token on the IPC socket, where there is no untrusted client to gate:

    hyprctl activationtoken | makoctl invoke --token-stdin

No authority is added. Anything that can reach that socket can already run
`hyprctl dispatch focuswindow`, which focuses unconditionally, where
CWindow::activate() still honours misc:focus_on_activate, per-window
suppressevent rules, and no-ops on unmapped windows. The token is single-use,
expires in 10s rather than the 12 months a client token gets, and IPC-minted
tokens are capped at 10 the same way a client's are.

Token goes over stdin, not argv: it is a bearer credential and argv is readable
by any same-uid process via /proc/<pid>/cmdline.

The keybind shape-checks the token before forwarding. That is not paranoia --
an hyprctl predating this patch answers "unknown request" on *stdout* with exit
0, so an unguarded pipe would forward that as the token and suppress mako's own
fallback mint. Verified all three branches (unknown request, real UUID, empty)
against stubs.

Verified: both patches apply to pristine v0.56.2 / mako 1.11.0; mako builds
under -Wall -Wextra -Werror and forwards a supplied token verbatim (confirmed
on the bus). The Hyprland patch is NOT compile-verified locally -- CI is the
build check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
MSG

content.text:
Two consecutive clean rounds over unchanged HEAD (`c2121679`), four angles each, **zero Critical or Important**. Two nits, both by design:

- *mako doesn't validate token format* — correct: token formats are compositor-specific, so mako forwards verbatim and the shape check lives in the keybind where the compositor is known.
- *`read_token` truncates past 511 bytes* — a UUID is 36; a truncated malformed input yields a token the compositor ignores.
